# MemoryCoreRecorderService identity-projection spec is flaky — third CI occurrence in one day

## Context

`test/playwright/unit/ai/services/memory-core/MemoryCoreRecorderService.spec.mjs:704` — `independently downgrades the identity projection when its writer status is partial` — flaked for the third time on 2026-08-12, each time recovering on retry while costing a full red/rerun cycle on an unrelated PR.

## Evidence

- Third occurrence: run `31643257591` (PR #17040, a diff that does not touch Memory Core at all): first attempt failed `expect(metrics.reembedRatio).toMatchObject({status: 'partial', reason: 'embedding-identity-writer-partial'})` at line 732, passed on in-run retry (`1 flaky`), and its worker collateral produced `1 error was not a part of any test` + `1 did not run`, turning a 13,000-pass run red.
- Two earlier same-day occurrences were absorbed as rerun-and-pass (recorded in Memory Core session context); the standing commitment was that a third occurrence earns this ticket.

## The Problem

The assertion expects the `reembedRatio` projection to be `partial` at the observation moment; intermittently the projection reads `ok`, which suggests the fixture observes the projection before (or after) the writer-status downgrade settles — an ordering/timing dependency inside the fixture, not a production defect signal so far.

## The Fix (owner to verify, not prescribe)

Make the arm deterministic: either drive the writer-status transition synchronously through an injected seam, or await the exact settlement signal the projection derives from before asserting. If investigation instead reveals a real race in the projection derivation, that becomes the finding and the fix moves to production code.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Root cause named (fixture ordering vs production race) with evidence.
- [ ] The spec passes 50 consecutive local iterations (`--repeat-each`) after the fix.
- [ ] No production behavior change without its own justification.

PR #17040 (victim run) · epic-adjacent CI hygiene

* feat(ai): make the embedding retry backoff base a leaf so specs stop paying it (#17124)

The backoff was hardcoded 2 ** retries * 1000, so every spec exercising a retry
paid the production delay in real wall-clock. Tests then worked around the
symptom rather than the cause: the leaseYield spec shrank maxRetries because a
five-retry mutation run exhausted its timeout, which trades coverage for seconds
and quietly asserts a shallower retry than production ships.

The base is now kb.backoffBaseMs, default 1000, sibling to the existing
memoryWal.backoffBaseMs and messageWal.backoffBaseMs leaves - same default, same
role, so the three read alike rather than coining a third spelling.

The test pin lives in the unit Playwright config beside UNIT_TEST_MODE, not in
the leaf: an inline branch inside leaf(...) bakes imperative env-resolution into
the declarative SSOT, and a per-spec write mutates a shared singleton. The env
layer is the sanctioned seam.

Measured on test/playwright/unit/ai/services/knowledge-base/, 649 tests passing
in both arms:

  before  15.9s
  after    9.6s

Scope correction: VectorService has ONE backoff site, not the two the ticket
names. grep -c setTimeout returns 1; the second cited line is carried-prefix
embedding-binding validation, which throws and never sleeps.

* feat(build): require a fixed second-scale wait to name what it waits for (#17124)

The visible shape is a bare setTimeout in a spec and the visible cost is wall
clock, but the bare sleep is a symptom. In every censused site the spec was
out-waiting a HARDCODED PRODUCTION CONSTANT it had no way to inject - a poll
interval, a lock-hold threshold, a token TTL, a spawn startup delay. A test
cannot pin what the source does not expose, so it guesses a number larger than
the constant and pays it forever.

So the rule is not "no sleeps": a fixed second-scale wait must carry either
`wall-clock-under-test:` or `out-waits: <the constant>`. Naming it is cheap, and
the naming IS the census that finds the next non-injectable constant.

Deleting a sleep is explicitly NOT the sanctioned fix, and the failure text says
so. Measured on the wake daemon spec: readiness is 90ms against sleeps waiting
1000ms, converting a sleep to a readiness poll moved 6.4s to 6.3s, and DELETING
one moved 6.4s to 12.2s with every assertion still green - the wall clock is
quantized by the production poll interval, so removing the wait pushes injection
before the next watermark and costs a whole extra cycle. A guard that nudges
toward the wrong repair converts a visible cost into an invisible one and prints
green.

Three sites earned annotations rather than baseline rows, which is the escape
hatch working: an outbox lock-hold threshold, a token TTL boundary, and
spawnBridge's 2000ms startupDelayMs - the last named by the spec's own comment.
Each names a leaf candidate.

The remaining 83 are baselined PER SITE, not per file: these convert rather than
vanish (a sleep becomes a readiness poll), and a file count would silently
absorb a conversion that left the site present. A stale row fails too, so the
baseline may only shrink.

Controls: a new unjustified sleep fails with the site named; a baseline row
without a live site fails; the intact tree passes at 83 baselined, 0 new,
0 stale. Mirrored in CI so --no-verify cannot bypass it; guard-ci-parity green.

* fix(build): report the leaf-candidate backlog so a zeroed baseline cannot read as speed (#17124)

Found by the author of the largest affected spec while reviewing this guard:
every one of her 83 sites would TRUTHFULLY earn `out-waits: POLL_INTERVAL_MS`.
Annotating them is the correct local action, and it drives the baseline to zero
while recovering zero wall clock. A burndown that completes without the suite
getting one millisecond faster is precisely the metric-moves-goal-doesn't shape
this guard exists to prevent - reappearing inside the guard itself.

The rule is not wrong; the reading was. The baseline measures ANNOTATION DEBT,
not wall clock. So the guard now reports a second number with the opposite
meaning: `out-waits:` sites are discharged AND recorded as backlog, because both
are true at once - the wait is accounted for, and the constant it names is still
hardcoded, so the time is still being paid.

Both counts print together on success rather than the distinction living only in
a docstring, because a reader consumes the printed line. A rising backlog is a
finding, not a failure; it falling means a constant became injectable, which is
the repair that actually removes wall clock.

Concretely: annotating the 83 would empty the baseline and raise the backlog to
~86 sites / ~90s, making the unrecovered time MORE visible rather than less.

* fix(ai): convert the SECOND backoff site — my census predated the rebase (#17124)

Retraction: the ticket said two backoff sites and I said one. The ticket was
right. My grep ran before this branch rebased onto #17120, which is the PR that
ADDED the carried-prefix write retry - so the second site did not exist on the
tree I censused, and the rebase then carried it in silently while my commit
message and PR body claimed a one-site census.

A census is only valid against the tree it ran on. Rebasing invalidates it as
surely as an edit does, and nothing re-ran it because the claim had already been
written down.

Both sites now read the leaf. They are in the same function with backoffBaseMs
already destructured at :1017, so the second needed no plumbing - only noticing.

Also repaired, both consequences of the leaf that CI caught and I had not run
locally before pushing:

- config-leaf-parity snapshot regenerated for the added declared path, committed
  in the same commit so the addition stays reviewable.
- retry-bound-registry re-keyed: changing the expression text changed both site
  hashes, so the entries went stale and the sites read UNCLASSIFIED. Both

* fix(build): count occurrences, skip prose, and stop smuggling a field on an array (#17124)

The baseline keyed on file+text as a SET, so 64 byte-identical `setTimeout(resolve, 1000)`
lines collapsed to one entry and removing 63 of them left the key matching, nothing stale,
and the guard green. Counting occurrences restores site granularity without keying on line
numbers, which shift under any edit above them.

Prose mentions of the pattern — this guard's own docstrings, its spec's fixtures — are not
sleeps and no longer count as them.

The backlog total rode as a property smuggled onto the returned array, where it survived
every array operation that rebuilt the list. It is a field on an object now.

* fix(build): the sleep guard reads every candidate, and reads delays by value (#17124)

@neo-gpt found two executable bypasses by reading the matcher instead of trusting its green
run against the tree — the most expensive kind of hole, because the gate prints OK while
letting the class through.

- `SLEEP_RE.exec(text)` without `/g` returns the LEFTMOST match, so a sub-threshold call
  earlier on the same line consumed the line's only inspection and the real site behind it was
  never examined. A gate that stops at the first thing it sees is a sample of size one.
- `(\d+)` cannot match `1_000` or `1e3` at all. Both are ordinary JavaScript spellings of this
  exact threshold, so they were invisible rather than mis-measured. The capture is now a
  numeric literal and the delay is compared by VALUE: the subject is how long a spec waits,
  never how the author spelled it.

Controls, on a disk fixture rather than inline — this spec's own noise-control asserts that
THIS file yields nothing, and embedding real call sites here would make two correct tests
contradict each other. Each half was mutation-verified as its own variable: with the narrow
capture restored the fixture yields only `[5000]`; with leftmost-only inspection restored it
loses the shadowed site. The mirror case is covered too — a `1e3` wait carrying a marker is
still discharged, because widening what the guard can SEE must not widen what it REFUSES.

83 baselined, 0 new, 0 stale against the real tree; 765 tests green across the guard, the
workflow-parity spec, and the restored buildScripts suites.

Co-Authored-By: Euclid <neo-gpt@neomjs.com>

* fix(ai): the backoff base takes the delay domain, not the loose numeric one (#17124)

`'number'` accepted a negative base — and `base * 2 ** n` with a negative base schedules every
retry in the past, so the backoff silently stops being a backoff. It accepted fractional values
too, which yield sub-millisecond timers the runtime rounds on its own terms, leaving the
configured ladder and the observed one to diverge with nothing reporting it. `nonNegativeInt`
is the domain this config already defines for delays where zero is legitimate.

@neo-gpt caught the domain; the interesting part is why it was wrong. The PR body defended
`'number'` as matching `memoryWal.backoffBaseMs` and `messageWal.backoffBaseMs` — and that
claim is TRUE, both siblings spell it that way. But `batchDelay`, a delay leaf 57 lines above
this one in the same block, already used `nonNegativeInt`. Two precedents were in reach and I
matched the one that was consistent rather than the one that was correct, which is how a wrong
shape spreads by adjacency: the next site copies whichever neighbour it lands nearest.

Coverage follows the block's existing idiom on a fresh provider — the harness's own `1`ms pin
in the valid case, `-1` and `1.5` refused to the default in the invalid one. Mutation-verified:
under `'number'` the refusal case receives `-1` instead of the default.

The two WAL siblings carry the same loose domain. They are a different server's contract
surface and outside this ticket's ledger, so they get their own ticket rather than a silent
widening of this diff.

Co-Authored-By: Euclid <neo-gpt@neomjs.com>

* fix(build): stop enumerating literal spellings and let Number decide (#17124)

@neo-gpt's re-review: the widened pattern still missed `0x3e8`, `0o1750`, `0b1111101000`,
`1000.` and `.1e4` — five more legal spellings of this exact threshold, invisible to the gate.

This pattern has now been wrong twice in the same direction, which is the finding. First
`(\d+)` missed separators and exponentials; then a decimal-shaped replacement missed radix
prefixes and boundary dots. Enumerating spellings loses to the language, because the language
keeps having more of them, and each round only fixes the ones its author happened to think of.

So the delay is captured as a permissive token and `Number` decides — `Number` IS the parser
the runtime applies to this argument, so the guard's reach now equals the language's rather
than my imagination's. Identifiers and calls yield NaN and are skipped, which is the verdict a
stricter pattern reached by failing to match; a named-constant control pins that, because a
loose match must not become a match-everything.

The worst part is that the module already said this. `toMs`'s docblock argued for delegating
to `Number` as "the same parser the runtime uses" while the regex beside it kept hand-rolling
the grammar — correct prose over an implementation that only half applied it.

All nine spellings verified against the real parser and covered as controls; mutation-verified
against the prior pattern, which misses exactly the five named. 83 baselined, 0 new, 0 stale
on the real tree — the wider grammar exposes no hidden sites, so the baseline is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Euclid <neo-gpt@neomjs.com>

* fix(build): a census expires when its tree moves, and a partial conversion is reduced not deleted (#17124)

Two defects, both surfaced by rebasing this branch onto a `dev` that moved under it.

The baseline claimed 64 occurrences of the one-second wait in `daemon.spec.mjs`.
`dev` holds 63: `16a26b5d53` (#17128) removed one after this branch's merge base.
`reconcile()` reads an over-permissive row as stale and exits 1, so this branch was
red on merge with nothing else involved — its own CI stayed green only because it
ran against the base where 64 was still true. A baseline is a measurement pinned to
a tree, and nothing here noticed the tree move.

The stale message then prescribed the wrong remedy for the common case. It said
"Remove these rows", which is right only when a row lost EVERY site. Deleting a
partially converted row un-accounts the sites it still legitimately grandfathers,
and they re-enter as `fresh` — the guard fails from the other side and reports a
conversion back to its author as a regression. `reconcile()` already computed the
surplus but never showed it; stale rows now carry `remaining` so the message can
name the two remedies apart.

* feat(build): require a fixed second-scale wait to name what it waits for (#17124)

The visible shape is a bare setTimeout in a spec and the visible cost is wall
clock, but the bare sleep is a symptom. In every censused site the spec was
out-waiting a HARDCODED PRODUCTION CONSTANT it had no way to inject - a poll
interval, a lock-hold threshold, a token TTL, a spawn startup delay. A test
cannot pin what the source does not expose, so it guesses a number larger than
the constant and pays it forever.

So the rule is not "no sleeps": a fixed second-scale wait must carry either
`wall-clock-under-test:` or `out-waits: <the constant>`. Naming it is cheap, and
the naming IS the census that finds the next non-injectable constant.

Deleting a sleep is explicitly NOT the sanctioned fix, and the failure text says
so. Measured on the wake daemon spec: readiness is 90ms against sleeps waiting
1000ms, converting a sleep to a readiness poll moved 6.4s to 6.3s, and DELETING
one moved 6.4s to 12.2s with every assertion still green - the wall clock is
quantized by the production poll interval, so removing the wait pushes injection
before the next watermark and costs a whole extra cycle. A guard that nudges
toward the wrong repair converts a visible cost into an invisible one and prints
green.

Three sites earned annotations rather than baseline rows, which is the escape
hatch working: an outbox lock-hold threshold, a token TTL boundary, and
spawnBridge's 2000ms startupDelayMs - the last named by the spec's own comment.
Each names a leaf candidate.

The remaining 83 are baselined PER SITE, not per file: these convert rather than
vanish (a sleep becomes a readiness poll), and a file count would silently
absorb a conversion that left the site present. A stale row fails too, so the
baseline may only shrink.

Controls: a new unjustified sleep fails with the site named; a baseline row
without a live site fails; the intact tree passes at 83 baselined, 0 new,
0 stale. Mirrored in CI so --no-verify cannot bypass it; guard-ci-parity green.

* fix(build): report the leaf-candidate backlog so a zeroed baseline cannot read as speed (#17124)

Found by the author of the largest affected spec while reviewing this guard:
every one of her 83 sites would TRUTHFULLY earn `out-waits: POLL_INTERVAL_MS`.
Annotating them is the correct local action, and it drives the baseline to zero
while recovering zero wall clock. A burndown that completes without the suite
getting one millisecond faster is precisely the metric-moves-goal-doesn't shape
this guard exists to prevent - reappearing inside the guard itself.

The rule is not wrong; the reading was. The baseline measures ANNOTATION DEBT,
not wall clock. So the guard now reports a second number with the opposite
meaning: `out-waits:` sites are discharged AND recorded as backlog, because both
are true at once - the wait is accounted for, and the constant it names is still
hardcoded, so the time is still being paid.

Both counts print together on success rather than the distinction living only in
a docstring, because a reader consumes the printed line. A rising backlog is a
finding, not a failure; it falling means a constant became injectable, which is
the repair that actually removes wall clock.

Concretely: annotating the 83 would empty the baseline and raise the backlog to
~86 sites / ~90s, making the unrecovered time MORE visible rather than less.

* fix(ai): convert the SECOND backoff site — my census predated the rebase (#17124)

Retraction: the ticket said two backoff sites and I said one. The ticket was
right. My grep ran before this branch rebased onto #17120, which is the PR that
ADDED the carried-prefix write retry - so the second site did not exist on the
tree I censused, and the rebase then carried it in silently while my commit
message and PR body claimed a one-site census.

A census is only valid against the tree it ran on. Rebasing invalidates it as
surely as an edit does, and nothing re-ran it because the claim had already been
written down.

Both sites now read the leaf. They are in the same function with backoffBaseMs
already destructured at :1017, so the second needed no plumbing - only noticing.

Also repaired, both consequences of the leaf that CI caught and I had not run
locally before pushing:

- config-leaf-parity snapshot regenerated for the added declared path, committed
  in the same commit so the addition stays reviewable.
- retry-bound-registry re-keyed: changing the expression text changed both site
  hashes, so the entries went stale and the sites read UNCLASSIFIED. Both
  classifications are preserved verbatim - the bound is unchanged, since the
  base scales the delay and never the attempt count - with a note recording that
  the base is now a leaf. Both lines are textually identical now, hence the
  a17aac7c / a17aac7c#1 disambiguation; the write arm is :1131 and the embed arm
  is :1235, mapped by their existing witnesses rather than by position.

* fix(build): register the guard's workflow and stop its import from exiting the process (#17124)

CI caught two things the local run could not, and the second is the worse one.

1. The new workflow was unregistered in lintWorkflowScanRootParity's registry,
so the scanned-subset-of-watched invariant had no entry for it. Registered with
source `imported` rather than `declared`, which required exporting SCAN_SURFACE -
the baseline belongs in that surface alongside the specs, because it is an INPUT
to the verdict and a run that does not re-trigger on a baseline edit would let a
site be blessed by editing the record of what exists.

2. Exporting SCAN_SURFACE made the module importable while its top-level body
still ran the whole lint and called process.exit(). Inside a Playwright worker
that exit killed the worker with NO failure message - the spec reported nothing
rather than reporting red, which is strictly worse than a normal failure because
nobody can see it. The body is now behind the direct-invocation guard the
sibling lint already uses.

Attribution for the other two unit failures on this head, checked rather than
assumed: knowledgeBaseArtifact:775 (RSS bound) and MemoryCoreRecorderService:708
both pass locally on this branch, 67/67. The first is a memory bound that only
breaks under CI parallel load; the second is the known identity-projection flake
already tracked by #17043. Neither is this diff.

* fix(build): count occurrences, skip prose, and stop smuggling a field on an array (#17124)

The baseline keyed on file+text as a SET, so 64 byte-identical `setTimeout(resolve, 1000)`
lines collapsed to one entry and removing 63 of them left the key matching, nothing stale,
and the guard green. Counting occurrences restores site granularity without keying on line
numbers, which shift under any edit above them.

Prose mentions of the pattern — this guard's own docstrings, its spec's fixtures — are not
sleeps and no longer count as them.

The backlog total rode as a property smuggled onto the returned array, where it survived
every array operation that rebuilt the list. It is a field on an object now.

* fix(build): the sleep guard reads every candidate, and reads delays by value (#17124)

@neo-gpt found two executable bypasses by reading the matcher instead of trusting its green
run against the tree — the most expensive kind of hole, because the gate prints OK while
letting the class through.

- `SLEEP_RE.exec(text)` without `/g` returns the LEFTMOST match, so a sub-threshold call
  earlier on the same line consumed the line's only inspection and the real site behind it was
  never examined. A gate that stops at the first thing it sees is a sample of size one.
- `(\d+)` cannot match `1_000` or `1e3` at all. Both are ordinary JavaScript spellings of this
  exact threshold, so they were invisible rather than mis-measured. The capture is now a
  numeric literal and the delay is compared by VALUE: the subject is how long a spec waits,
  never how the author spelled it.

Controls, on a disk fixture rather than inline — this spec's own noise-control asserts that
THIS file yields nothing, and embedding real call sites here would make two correct tests
contradict each other. Each half was mutation-verified as its own variable: with the narrow
capture restored the fixture yields only `[5000]`; with leftmost-only inspection restored it
loses the shadowed site. The mirror case is covered too — a `1e3` wait carrying a marker is
still discharged, because widening what the guard can SEE must not widen what it REFUSES.

83 baselined, 0 new, 0 stale against the real tree; 765 tests green across the guard, the
workflow-parity spec, and the restored buildScripts suites.

Co-Authored-By: Euclid <neo-gpt@neomjs.com>

* fix(ai): the backoff base takes the delay domain, not the loose numeric one (#17124)

`'number'` accepted a negative base — and `base * 2 ** n` with a negative base schedules every
retry in the past, so the backoff silently stops being a backoff. It accepted fractional values
too, which yield sub-millisecond timers the runtime rounds on its own terms, leaving the
configured ladder and the observed one to diverge with nothing reporting it. `nonNegativeInt`
is the domain this config already defines for delays where zero is legitimate.

@neo-gpt caught the domain; the interesting part is why it was wrong. The PR body defended
`'number'` as matching `memoryWal.backoffBaseMs` and `messageWal.backoffBaseMs` — and that
claim is TRUE, both siblings spell it that way. But `batchDelay`, a delay leaf 57 lines above
this one in the same block, already used `nonNegativeInt`. Two precedents were in reach and I
matched the one that was consistent rather than the one that was correct, which is how a wrong
shape spreads by adjacency: the next site copies whichever neighbour it lands nearest.

Coverage follows the block's existing idiom on a fresh provider — the harness's own `1`ms pin
in the valid case, `-1` and `1.5` refused to the default in the invalid one. Mutation-verified:
under `'number'` the refusal case receives `-1` instead of the default.

The two WAL siblings carry the same loose domain. They are a different server's contract
surface and outside this ticket's ledger, so they get their own ticket rather than a silent
widening of this diff.

Co-Authored-By: Euclid <neo-gpt@neomjs.com>

* fix(build): stop enumerating literal spellings and let Number decide (#17124)

@neo-gpt's re-review: the widened pattern still missed `0x3e8`, `0o1750`, `0b1111101000`,
`1000.` and `.1e4` — five more legal spellings of this exact threshold, invisible to the gate.

This pattern has now been wrong twice in the same direction, which is the finding. First
`(\d+)` missed separators and exponentials; then a decimal-shaped replacement missed radix
prefixes and boundary dots. Enumerating spellings loses to the language, because the language
keeps having more of them, and each round only fixes the ones its author happened to think of.

So the delay is captured as a permissive token and `Number` decides — `Number` IS the parser
the runtime applies to this argument, so the guard's reach now equals the language's rather
than my imagination's. Identifiers and calls yield NaN and are skipped, which is the verdict a
stricter pattern reached by failing to match; a named-constant control pins that, because a
loose match must not become a match-everything.

The worst part is that the module already said this. `toMs`'s docblock argued for delegating
to `Number` as "the same parser the runtime uses" while the regex beside it kept hand-rolling
the grammar — correct prose over an implementation that only half applied it.

All nine spellings verified against the real parser and covered as controls; mutation-verified
against the prior pattern, which misses exactly the five named. 83 baselined, 0 new, 0 stale
on the real tree — the wider grammar exposes no hidden sites, so the baseline is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Euclid <neo-gpt@neomjs.com>

* fix(build): a census expires when its tree moves, and a partial conversion is reduced not deleted (#17124)

Two defects, both surfaced by rebasing this branch onto a `dev` that moved under it.

The baseline claimed 64 occurrences of the one-second wait in `daemon.spec.mjs`.
`dev` holds 63: `c0447c2ce3` (#17128) removed one after this branch's merge base.
`reconcile()` reads an over-permissive row as stale and exits 1, so this branch was
red on merge with nothing else involved — its own CI stayed green only because it
ran against the base where 64 was still true. A baseline is a measurement pinned to
a tree, and nothing here noticed the tree move.

The stale message then prescribed the wrong remedy for the common case. It said
"Remove these rows", which is right only when a row lost EVERY site. Deleting a
partially converted row un-accounts the sites it still legitimately grandfathers,
and they re-enter as `fresh` — the guard fails from the other side and reports a
conversion back to its author as a regression. `reconcile()` already computed the
surplus but never showed it; stale rows now carry `remaining` so the message can
name the two remedies apart.

Co-Authored-By: Ada <neo-opus-4-7@neomjs.com>
